newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Independents take Australia close to Telstra sale.
newsitem.headline: Independents take Australia close to Telstra sale.

text.p: Australia looked set on Thursday to go ahead with its biggest ever privatisation after key independent politicians declared the government had a mandate to sell a third of telecoms carrier Telstra Corp.

"I do not see my role, nor do I see the Senate's role, to be obstructionist of government policy for which they've got a mandate at the election," independent senator Brian Harradine told reporters as the A$8 billion (US$6.4 billion) sale moved towards a final vote on Monday.

Prime Minister John Howard's government also sweetened its lure, making new offers aimed at the demands of Harradine and fellow independent Mal Colston, who together represent the only potential source of the two votes that the government needs.

The government said the sale would pay for a A$1.1 billion environmental repair fund -- up from the originally promised A$1 billion -- and there would be a new A$250 million fund to help develop telecommunications jobs in rural areas.

Harradine himself revealed a deal with the government that answered another of his objections. No sale would go ahead until a committee examined his proposal to raise A$8 billion by selling Telstra securities, rather than equity, he said.
The government is two votes short of a majority in the Senate, and every non-government senator except the two independents is against the sale.

"We will vote against it until the very end according to our principles and I do urge senators Colston and Harradine to reconsider," Cheryl Kernot, the leader of the minority Democrats, told reporters.
But Labor opposition leader Kim Beazley gave up hope of stopping the sale, saying it had become innevitable in March when the country installed a conservative government.
"They voted for a government that would do it and therefore it's done," Beazley said.

Labor itself privatised many government businesses in its 13 years of power, including Qantas Airways Ltd, but says that Telstra has strong monopolistic powers and should therefore remain in public hands.
Telstra, originally an outgrowth of the post office, was highly unpopular when it enjoyed a complete monopoly. One old joke defined Soviet-style communism as Telstra with tanks.
But the company has lifted its game since a competitor, Optus Communications, began operations in the early 1990s, although the government company still dominates the market.
Despite the Liberal-National government's landslide election win and Telstra's traditional unpopularity, opinion polls consistently show that reform-weary voters oppose the partial privatisation.
